title: The symmetric algebra is graded by the images of the tensor powers
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-module. Let $\mathrm T_R(M)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathrm T^n_R(M)$ be the tensor algebra ($\mathrm T^0_R(M)=R$, $\mathrm T^n_R(M)=M^{\otimes_R n}$), $J\subseteq\mathrm T_R(M)$ the two-sided ideal generated by the elements $x\otimes y-y\otimes x$ ($x,y\in M$), $\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)=\mathrm T_R(M)/J$ with quotient map $\pi$, and $\iota_M=\pi|_M:M\to\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)$ [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-universal-property]. For $n\ge0$ let $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)=\pi(\mathrm T^n_R(M))$, the $R$-submodule of $\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)$ spanned by the products $\iota_M(x_1)\cdots\iota_M(x_n)$ with $x_1,\dots,x_n\in M$ (so $\operatorname{Sym}^0_R(M)=R\cdot1$ and $\operatorname{Sym}^1_R(M)=\iota_M(M)$). Then $J=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}(J\cap\mathrm T^n_R(M))$, and consequently $\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$ as $R$-modules: every element of $\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)$ is a finite sum $\sum_n s_n$ with $s_n\in\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$, and the $s_n$ are uniquely determined by it. Moreover $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)\cdot\operatorname{Sym}^m_R(M)\subseteq\operatorname{Sym}^{n+m}_R(M)$ for all $n,m\ge0$.

source.place: Algebra, Section 00DM (section-tensor-algebra, line 2165): T(M) is the direct sum of the T^n(M) with T^n * T^m in T^{n+m}; Sym(M) is the quotient of T(M) by the two-sided ideal generated by the degree-2 elements x (x) y - y (x) x, and Sym^n(M) is the image of T^n(M) (the text writes 'the image of a pure tensor x_1 (x) ... (x) x_n in Sym^n(M)'); the grading of the quotient by an ideal generated by homogeneous elements is used there without statement

proof.text: (The grading of $\mathrm T_R(M)$.) By [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-algebra-graded], $\mathrm T_R(M)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathrm T^n_R(M)$, where $\mathrm T^n_R(M)$ is the $R$-submodule spanned by the pure tensors $x_1\otimes\dots\otimes x_n=\iota(x_1)\cdots\iota(x_n)$, $\mathrm T^0_R(M)=R\cdot1$, $\mathrm T^1_R(M)=M$, and $\mathrm T^n_R(M)\cdot\mathrm T^m_R(M)\subseteq\mathrm T^{n+m}_R(M)$. For $t\in\mathrm T_R(M)$ write $\mathrm{pr}_n(t)\in\mathrm T^n_R(M)$ for its degree-$n$ component, so $t=\sum_n\mathrm{pr}_n(t)$ (finitely many nonzero), and $t=\sum_nt_n$ with $t_n\in\mathrm T^n_R(M)$ implies $t_n=\mathrm{pr}_n(t)$ for all $n$.

source.place: Algebra, Section 00DM (section-tensor-algebra, line 2165): definition of T(M) as the direct sum of the T^n(M) with concatenation product

proof.text: ($J$ is spanned by homogeneous elements of $J$.) Put $g(x,y)=x\otimes y-y\otimes x\in\mathrm T^2_R(M)$. The two-sided ideal $J$ generated by the $g(x,y)$ consists of the finite sums $\sum_{i}a_i\,g(x_i,y_i)\,b_i$ with $a_i,b_i\in\mathrm T_R(M)$, $x_i,y_i\in M$. Decompose $a_i=\sum_p\mathrm{pr}_p(a_i)$ and $b_i=\sum_q\mathrm{pr}_q(b_i)$ (Step 1) and expand by distributivity: every element of $J$ is a finite sum of elements $h=a\,g(x,y)\,b$ with $a\in\mathrm T^p_R(M)$, $b\in\mathrm T^q_R(M)$ for some $p,q\ge0$. Each such $h$ lies in $J$ ($J$ is a two-sided ideal containing $g(x,y)$) and in $\mathrm T^{p+2+q}_R(M)$ (apply $\mathrm T^p\cdot\mathrm T^2\subseteq\mathrm T^{p+2}$ and $\mathrm T^{p+2}\cdot\mathrm T^q\subseteq\mathrm T^{p+2+q}$ from [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-algebra-graded]). So every $j\in J$ is a finite sum $j=\sum_kh_k$ with $h_k\in J\cap\mathrm T^{d_k}_R(M)$ for some degrees $d_k$.

source.place: Algebra, Section 00DM (section-tensor-algebra, line 2165); the grading of Sym(M) is used there without statement and without proof; Sym(M) is defined there as T(M) modulo the two-sided ideal generated by the degree-2 elements x (x) y - y (x) x

proof.text: ($J=\bigoplus_n(J\cap\mathrm T^n_R(M))$.) Let $j\in J$ and write $j=\sum_kh_k$ as in Step 2. For each $n$ put $j_n=\sum_{k:\,d_k=n}h_k$; it lies in $J$ (a sum of elements of $J$) and in $\mathrm T^n_R(M)$, and $j=\sum_nj_n$. By the uniqueness of components (Step 1), $j_n=\mathrm{pr}_n(j)$. Hence $\mathrm{pr}_n(j)\in J\cap\mathrm T^n_R(M)$ for every $j\in J$ and every $n$, so $J=\sum_n(J\cap\mathrm T^n_R(M))$, and the sum is direct because the sum $\sum_n\mathrm T^n_R(M)$ is direct (Step 1).

source.place: Algebra, Section 00DM (section-tensor-algebra, line 2165); the grading of Sym(M) is used there without statement and without proof

proof.text: ($\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$ and its spanning set.) $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)=\pi(\mathrm T^n_R(M))$ is an $R$-submodule of $\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)$, $\pi$ being $R$-linear. As $\pi$ is a ring homomorphism and $\iota_M=\pi|_M$ [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-universal-property], $\pi(x_1\otimes\dots\otimes x_n)=\pi(\iota(x_1))\cdots\pi(\iota(x_n))=\iota_M(x_1)\cdots\iota_M(x_n)$; since these pure tensors span $\mathrm T^n_R(M)$ (Step 1), their images span $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$. From $\mathrm T^0_R(M)=R\cdot1$ and $\mathrm T^1_R(M)=\iota(M)$ we get $\operatorname{Sym}^0_R(M)=R\cdot1$ and $\operatorname{Sym}^1_R(M)=\iota_M(M)$.

source.place: Algebra, Section 00DM (section-tensor-algebra, line 2165): 'The image of a pure tensor x_1 (x) ... (x) x_n in Sym^n(M) is denoted x_1 ... x_n. These elements generate Sym^n(M)'

proof.text: (Existence of the decomposition.) Let $s\in\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)$. As $\pi$ is surjective, $s=\pi(t)$ for some $t\in\mathrm T_R(M)$, and $t=\sum_n\mathrm{pr}_n(t)$ (Step 1) gives $s=\sum_n\pi(\mathrm{pr}_n(t))$, a finite sum with $\pi(\mathrm{pr}_n(t))\in\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$.

source.place: Algebra, Section 00DM (section-tensor-algebra, line 2165); the grading of Sym(M) is used there without statement and without proof

proof.text: (Uniqueness of the decomposition.) Suppose $\sum_ns_n=\sum_ns'_n$ with $s_n,s'_n\in\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$, finitely many nonzero. For each $n$ with $s_n\ne s'_n$ choose $t_n\in\mathrm T^n_R(M)$ with $\pi(t_n)=s_n-s'_n$ (possible as $s_n-s'_n\in\pi(\mathrm T^n_R(M))$), and put $t_n=0$ otherwise. Then $t=\sum_nt_n$ satisfies $\pi(t)=0$, i.e. $t\in J$. By uniqueness of components in $\mathrm T_R(M)$ (Step 1) $t_n=\mathrm{pr}_n(t)$, and by Step 3 $\mathrm{pr}_n(t)\in J$; hence $s_n-s'_n=\pi(t_n)=0$ for every $n$. Together with Step 5, $\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$ as $R$-modules.

source.place: Algebra, Section 00DM (section-tensor-algebra, line 2165); the grading of Sym(M) is used there without statement and without proof

proof.text: (Multiplicativity.) Let $s\in\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$, $s'\in\operatorname{Sym}^m_R(M)$, say $s=\pi(t)$, $s'=\pi(t')$ with $t\in\mathrm T^n_R(M)$, $t'\in\mathrm T^m_R(M)$. Then $ss'=\pi(tt')$ with $tt'\in\mathrm T^{n+m}_R(M)$ [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-algebra-graded], so $ss'\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n+m}_R(M)$; as $\operatorname{Sym}^{n+m}_R(M)$ is an $R$-submodule, it also contains the $R$-span of these products, so $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)\cdot\operatorname{Sym}^m_R(M)\subseteq\operatorname{Sym}^{n+m}_R(M)$.
